note: Each item links to an archive or publisher page that was opened and checked for a clear tie to the neighborhood; summaries paraphrase only what that page states. Pages that refuse our research agent are not read through mirrors or other tools: The People's Archive and Smithsonian sites are listed as archives to search, not as entries.

petworth.title: Memories of Community Change at "Celebrate Petworth"
petworth.summary: Humanities Truck blog post on recording short oral histories with residents at the 2019 Celebrate Petworth festival at 8th and Upshur, covering memories and changes seen over time, plus a home interview on Varnum Street with a woman who moved to Petworth in the 1940s.

petworth.title: Celebrate Petworth Festival 2019
petworth.summary: Archive collection of interviews and images gathered by the Humanities Truck at the 2019 Celebrate Petworth neighborhood festival.
petworth.archive: Humanities Truck Community Archive, American University Archives

petworth.title: Celebrate Petworth Festival 2021
petworth.summary: Interviews and images from the September 25, 2021 Celebrate Petworth festival, plus interviews with Petworth residents collected before the event.
petworth.archive: Humanities Truck Community Archive, American University Archives

petworth.title: Celebrate Petworth Festival 2022
petworth.summary: Archive collection of interviews and images from the 2022 Celebrate Petworth neighborhood festival.
petworth.archive: Humanities Truck Community Archive, American University Archives

petworth.title: Petworth Library 2019 - It's a Small World After All
petworth.summary: Records of a 2019 program at the Petworth library branch on DC history, public art and storytelling, where the Humanities Truck team also gathered oral histories from Petworth residents about how the neighborhood has changed.
petworth.archive: Humanities Truck Community Archive, American University Archives

petworth.title: Found at the library: One woman's remembrance of growing up in 1920s Petworth
petworth.summary: Petworth News post on a 1995 written memoir held by DC Public Library covering 1919-1950: her family home on Taylor Street, Petworth and Roosevelt schools, Upshur Street shops, the York Theater, streetcars, and the 1922 Knickerbocker snowstorm.
petworth.archive: Petworth News (memoir held at DC Public Library)

tenleytown.title: Joan Taylor
tenleytown.summary: She recalls Tenleytown as a Black community during her Deal and Wilson years, with wooden houses now gone near Nebraska Avenue and Reno Road, and Wilson High School during desegregation in the late 1950s. Also mentions Sears and Woodward and Lothrop on Wisconsin Avenue.

tenleytown.title: Timothy Hannapel and Emily Swartz
tenleytown.summary: Nephew and aunt discuss the Fort Reno concert series, a 1984 dig in Fort Reno Park, Wilson High School in the 1970s, neighborhood planning council youth programs, and the clearing of the largely Black Reno City community for Deal and Wilson. Includes 1983 photos of bands at Fort Reno.

tenleytown.title: Judith Clark Adams
tenleytown.summary: Adams recalls drug use around Fort Reno Park in the 1970s and the later concerts there, Wilson High School during busing and integration, Woodies in Friendship Heights, and teen hangouts on Wisconsin Avenue.

tenleytown.title: Richard Sullivan and John Sullivan
tenleytown.summary: Brothers recall streetcars to Friendship Heights (Richard thinks the last ran in 1962), working at the Woodward and Lothrop store there, Black families living around Tenleytown near Belt Road, and a year at Wilson High School.

tenleytown.title: James Fisher and Tanya Hardy
tenleytown.summary: Descendants of George Pointer trace the family's move from Broad Branch Road to Davenport Street in Reno City, a relative who attended the segregated Reno School, and an undertaker uncle who served the Fort Reno neighborhood.

tenleytown.title: Oral History of Rock Creek Baptist Church Members Recount Life at Reno City and along Broad Branch Road
tenleytown.who: Mary Daniel, Augusta Moore, and Eddie Dixon
tenleytown.summary: A 1977 recording with members of Rock Creek Baptist Church about life in Reno City, the Black community once at today's Fort Reno Park, and along Broad Branch Road. Offered as a downloadable PDF.

tenleytown.title: Wilson High School Videotaped Oral Histories
tenleytown.who: Tom Hier, Ken Luchs, Joan Topalian, Lisa Friedman, and members of the Class of 1954
tenleytown.summary: Videotaped oral histories with Woodrow Wilson High School graduates: a group recording by the Class of 1954 at its 60th reunion and individual interviews with alumni from the classes of 1956, 1961, 1965 and 1976.

tenleytown.title: [Your Band] Played Here (An Oral History of Fort Reno)
tenleytown.summary: Washington City Paper oral history, compiled from interviews, of the free summer concert series at Fort Reno in Tenleytown, from its 1968 start through the punk and hardcore years to the early 2010s, with organizers, volunteers and musicians.

tenleytown.title: Fort Reno's Oral History: Saint George
tenleytown.summary: Companion piece to the City Paper's Fort Reno oral history: organizers and musicians remember Father George Dennis, the Jesuit priest who guided the concert series for decades.

tenleytown.title: 4941 Butterworth Place, NW
tenleytown.summary: Recollection, tagged oral history, of growing up from 1910 in a then-rural house near today's AU Park. The family went to Tenleytown for shopping, school and church by way of Murdock Mill Road and Wisconsin Avenue.

tenleytown.title: The Destruction of Reno City
tenleytown.summary: Boundary Stones article on Reno City, the largely Black community at Fort Reno in Tenleytown, and its removal by the late 1940s. Draws on 1977 interviews with former residents for daily life and the condemnation process.

gloverpark.title: “Toddy” Lyddane: Oral History
gloverpark.summary: Condensed from a 2010 interview for the Citizens Association of Georgetown oral history project. Lyddane, who lived on Hall Place until he was eighteen, recalls baseball in the street, lamplighters, trolleys downtown, the then-open Naval Observatory grounds, and band concerts and films at Mount Alto Hospital after World War I.
gloverpark.archive: Glover Park History (Carlton Fletcher), Oral History and Reminiscences

gloverpark.title: Margaret Woodward
gloverpark.summary: Excerpts from a 1988 U.S. Naval Observatory oral history, plus other pieces about her. Woodward moved to Hall Place as a small child around 1913, says the street was named for Mr. Hall who lived at its foot, and remembers playing with astronomers' children and treating the unlocked Observatory grounds, reached by Observatory Lane, as a private playground.
gloverpark.archive: Glover Park History (Carlton Fletcher), Oral History and Reminiscences

gloverpark.title: “Kelly” Brown: Gypsies in B.T. Woods
gloverpark.summary: From a 1969 oral history held in the Peabody Room of the Georgetown library. Brown, born in the Bryantown section of Georgetown, recalls a Romani encampment in the woods across from Georgetown Hospital; his mother and friends sewed clothes for a promised wedding and found the camp gone overnight. Fletcher cites 1911 press reports of a camp near Western High School.
gloverpark.archive: Glover Park History (Carlton Fletcher), Oral History and Reminiscences

gloverpark.title: Margaret Hunt: Childhood in Glover Park, 1926-1939
gloverpark.summary: Hunt moved to Tunlaw Road at age eight in 1926. She recalls the Piggly-Wiggly, Pearson's drugstore and the streetcar, a huge walnut tree at Calvert and Tunlaw she was told gave the road its name, and two old houses trucked across to Wisconsin Avenue around 1929-30 before Calvert Street was cut through.
gloverpark.archive: Glover Park History (Carlton Fletcher), Oral History and Reminiscences

gloverpark.title: Ellen McDowell Keyes: A Glover Park Childhood in the Twenties
gloverpark.summary: Born in 1920, Keyes lived on Hall Place until she was nine; first printed in the Glover Park Gazette in 2003. She remembers milk and Jewel Tea deliveries, a scissors grinder with a monkey, children chasing the ice wagon for chips, Pearson's Drug Store, Dacey's Deli, the Piggly-Wiggly, and street games with the gas lamp as home base.
gloverpark.archive: Glover Park History (Carlton Fletcher), Oral History and Reminiscences

gloverpark.title: Francis McKinley: Remembering Glover Park in the Forties
gloverpark.summary: First published in the Glover Park Gazette in 1998. McKinley describes wartime Glover Park: air-raid sirens sending children home from Tunlaw Road and Beecher Street, blackout shades checked by Civil Defense wardens, searchlights, service-star flags on doors, a severe housing shortage, and kindergarten sessions at Stoddert Elementary in 1942.
gloverpark.archive: Glover Park History (Carlton Fletcher), Oral History and Reminiscences

gloverpark.title: Grace Powell Cochran: Let’s Look Back
gloverpark.summary: Excerpts from an undated typescript in the Washingtoniana collection at the King Library. Cochran traces the first Tunlaw Road townhouses of 1918, a cornfield and frog pond across the street, her family's 1928 move along muddy Schneider's Lane (now Calvert Street), band concerts at Mount Alto Hospital and the shops near 37th and Wisconsin.
gloverpark.archive: Glover Park History (Carlton Fletcher), Oral History and Reminiscences

gloverpark.title: Paul Friday: Memories of Snow on W Street & “Suicide Hill”
gloverpark.summary: Friday recalls snow days in the early 1950s when police barricaded W Street between 38th and 39th for sledding, leaving a gap so children could sled off a small slope at the park they called Suicide Hill, and the city supplied a barrel fire at 39th and W where parents gathered.
gloverpark.archive: Glover Park History (Carlton Fletcher), Oral History and Reminiscences

gloverpark.title: Jennifer Williams Duffy: Beecher Street in the Thirties
gloverpark.summary: Duffy, who lived in Glover Park until she was thirteen, describes her block of Beecher Street as a 'doll's village' of narrow streets and brick rowhouses, where neighbors visited across porch railings without getting wet and she could name nearly everyone on the street.
gloverpark.archive: Glover Park History (Carlton Fletcher), Oral History and Reminiscences

gloverpark.title: Kathleen McCormick: B.T. Field
gloverpark.summary: McCormick, whose family moved to W Street in 1940, remembers city mule teams mowing the big field behind the houses, now Whitehaven Park, and being allowed to groom the mules at lunch. Fletcher adds that children called it B.T. Woods, likely for the old Bryantown settlement, and that a ball team used it in 1947.
gloverpark.archive: Glover Park History (Carlton Fletcher), Oral History and Reminiscences

georgetown.title: Virginia Luce Allen interview (part 1 of 2)
georgetown.summary: Allen (1919-2009), a fourth-generation Georgetowner, traces her mother's family back four generations in the neighborhood, describes a close-knit, racially mixed childhood community and how it changed, and explains how she founded the Georgetown Senior Center in 1981. The original cassette is in DC Public Library Special Collections.
georgetown.archive: DC Public Library Special Collections (St. Mary's Court Oral History Project), digitized copy on the Center for Knit and Crochet Digital Repository

georgetown.title: Longtime Residents Make Georgetown History Come Alive
georgetown.who: Frank Randolph, Barry Deutschman, Catherine Bowman, Georges Jacob, Don Shannon and Kay Evans
georgetown.summary: The Georgetowner's report on a Citizens Association of Georgetown oral history program. Speakers recalled school dogwood festivals, mixing prescriptions by hand at Morgan's Pharmacy, the segregated era when Black residents used Rose Park but not Volta Park, gas stations and gravel works on the postwar waterfront, and the Kennedy years.
georgetown.archive: Citizens Association of Georgetown Oral History Project (reported by The Georgetowner)

georgetown.title: Telling Georgetown’s Story, Person by Person
georgetown.who: Anne Emmet, Philip Levy, Richard Levy, Elizabeth Stevens and Gary Tischler
georgetown.summary: The Georgetowner's account of the third live presentation of CAG's oral history project. The Levy brothers recall growing up above the family store on M Street, a town of a dozen gas stations, and clubs like the Cellar Door; Anne Emmet remembers Volta Park as a junk heap; Elizabeth Stevens recalls shops such as Neam's Market.
georgetown.archive: Citizens Association of Georgetown Oral History Project (reported by The Georgetowner)

georgetown.title: ‘Town Crier’ Ray Kukulski Has Died
georgetown.summary: Obituary drawing on a long interview Kukulski gave CAG's oral history project in 2009. He recalled moving to 30th Street in 1967 with three fellow naval officers, when Geller's Lumber Yard and a railroad siding filled the area south of K Street, and later chairing the ANC as Washington Harbour transformed the waterfront.
georgetown.archive: Citizens Association of Georgetown Oral History Project (quoted in The Georgetowner)

georgetown.title: Henry recalls walking the streets and sidewalks of Georgetown
georgetown.summary: A short video story in the DC History Center's hometown DC exhibition. Musician Henry Rollins reflects on the late-1970s and 1980s punk and hardcore scene that turned Northwest businesses and sidewalks into creative spaces, and on how familiar Georgetown's streets still feel despite decades of change.

adamsmorgan.title: Adams Morgan History: Interviews with Residents
adamsmorgan.who: Olivia Cadaval, Carlos Arrien and Alicia Wilson, among others
adamsmorgan.summary: Video interviews accompanying the Adams Morgan History keepsake that Hola Cultura launched with the DC Oral History Collaborative in September 2019. Grouped as the early days, the community's blossoming, and a changing neighborhood, they trace the Latino community's growth, the role of the Latino Festival, and the area's later gentrification.
adamsmorgan.archive: Hola Cultura, with the DC Oral History Collaborative

adamsmorgan.title: Nancy on Fields of Plenty
adamsmorgan.summary: A short video story in the DC History Center's hometown DC exhibition. Shia recalls the food co-op run by the Adams Morgan Organization and how co-ops and farmers markets gave residents local, affordable groceries.

adamsmorgan.title: Arturo on bringing the Latin American Festival to the National Mall
adamsmorgan.summary: A short video story in the DC History Center's hometown DC exhibition. Griffiths describes how the Latino festival that began in the 1970s as a neighborhood gathering in Mount Pleasant and Adams Morgan grew by 1989 into a regional celebration on the National Mall.

adamsmorgan.title: Oral history interview with Randy K., 1967-
adamsmorgan.summary: Randy K. moved to D.C. in 1974 and grew up in Adams Morgan with his mother and four siblings. He describes being bullied, a Big Brothers match with Congressman Mickey Leland, watching Dupont Circle's gay clubs as a teenager, his 1986 HIV diagnosis, years of hardship, and later work as an advocate at HIPS.
adamsmorgan.archive: Rainbow History Project Oral History Collection

dupontcircle.title: Oral history interview with Sean Roach, 1951 -
dupontcircle.summary: Roach, a Georgetown University student from 1969 to 1973 who joined the Washington Gay Liberation Front in 1970, describes the group's activities, the relationship between the Gay Liberation Front House and its Dupont Circle neighbors, gay hangouts and bars, and job hunting as a gay man.
dupontcircle.archive: Rainbow History Project Oral History Collection

dupontcircle.title: Oral history interview with Helene Bloom, 1943-
dupontcircle.summary: Bloom, co-owner of Soho Tea & Coffee on P Street, describes Washington's LGBTQ community from 1974 on, marches for gay and women's causes in the late 1970s and early 1980s, and the bars, dance clubs and other LGBTQ spaces of Dupont Circle.
dupontcircle.archive: Rainbow History Project Oral History Collection

dupontcircle.title: Oral History Interview with Fran Levine, 1952-
dupontcircle.summary: Levine, Bloom's co-owner at Soho on P Street, describes changes in Dupont Circle from the late 1980s as an independent business owner, the neighborhood's LGBTQ bars and clubs and Soho as a gathering place, the community's response to AIDS, and the loss of gay gathering spaces.
dupontcircle.archive: Rainbow History Project Oral History Collection

dupontcircle.title: Oral history interview with Robert Miailovich
dupontcircle.summary: Miailovich, founder of Dignity-DC, discusses gay life and the Catholic group from the 1970s on. The recording ends with a short 2001 group segment with Darrell Trotman and Eric Newman, a couple of 30 years; the archive notes Trotman had lived in Dupont Circle since 1964.
dupontcircle.archive: Rainbow History Project Oral History Collection

dupontcircle.title: Oral History Interview with Tom Bower, 1948-
dupontcircle.summary: Recorded at Bower's home in the Dupont Circle neighborhood. An early organizer of Dignity's Washington chapter and a longtime Smithsonian museum worker, he talks about being both Catholic and gay, how D.C. Catholics embraced Dignity, and the times the church rejected it.
dupontcircle.archive: Rainbow History Project Oral History Collection

dupontcircle.title: Oral History Interview with William Wooby, 1947-
dupontcircle.summary: Wooby came from New York after Army service, worked at the gay clubs Lost and Found and Pier 9, and later owned The Collector Art Gallery Restaurant, first on U Street and then in Dupont Circle. He helped organize the 1989 artists' protest after the Corcoran canceled its Mapplethorpe show.
dupontcircle.archive: Rainbow History Project Oral History Collection

dupontcircle.title: Oral History with Mike Silverstein
dupontcircle.summary: Silverstein, a 30-year ABC News veteran who later served on the Dupont Circle ANC, recalls hearing about Stonewall on the news, meeting other gay Washingtonians at Lost & Found, and driving Frank Kameny in the 2010 Capital Pride Parade.
dupontcircle.archive: Rainbow History Project Oral History Collection

dupontcircle.title: Jane talks about the influence of Lambda Rising and its Book Report
dupontcircle.summary: A short video story in the DC History Center's hometown DC exhibition. Troxell recalls Lambda Rising, the Dupont Circle bookstore opened in 1974, and its Lambda Book Report, whose reviews helped publishers and readers take gay and lesbian authors seriously.

dupontcircle.title: Armonté reminisces about his Dad taking him to the Dupont Circle Snowball Fight
dupontcircle.summary: A short video story in the DC History Center's hometown DC exhibition. Butler remembers his father taking him to the annual Dupont Circle snowball fight that began after the 2010 Snowmageddon storm, and how those outings shaped his tie to the city.

clevelandpark.title: Lou Stovall Oral History
clevelandpark.summary: Interviewed by Kay Kohl. The printmaker recalls coming to Washington and Howard University, moving to Cleveland Park with his wife, artist Di Bagley Stovall, teaching silkscreen to neighborhood schoolchildren in their backyard studio, a Newark Street block party, and fears about fast traffic on Reno Road.

clevelandpark.title: Clare Tighe Oral History
clevelandpark.summary: Interviewed by Fran Maclean. Tighe's family moved to Ordway Street in 1960. She remembers Rosedale's open fields and fences, a neighbor's Icelandic pony, small family shops on Connecticut Avenue, and decorating cakes at the University Pastry Shop, and reflects on changes visible even in neighbors' gardens.

clevelandpark.title: George Idelson Oral History
clevelandpark.summary: Interviewed by CPHS board member Abigail Porter. Idelson, in Cleveland Park since 1967, explains moving to escape airport noise, calls the neighborhood intellectual and liberal, credits the 1986 historic district with preserving its character, and recalls fights over a Giant development and a proposed hillside village on Macomb Street.

clevelandpark.title: Cleveland Park Voices: A Social History (1984)
clevelandpark.who: Philip Stone, Elizabeth Faulkner, Mary Ellen Grogan and others
clevelandpark.summary: Interviews collected in 1984 by John Eaton students under Rives Carroll. Early residents recall a nearly rural place: Stone sledding down Macomb Street across Connecticut Avenue, Faulkner growing up at Rosedale, Grogan when Ordway was unpaved. Shopkeepers from the University Pastry Shop, Roma and Sullivan's also speak, as do residents of the war years.

clevelandpark.title: I am Cleveland Park: Preserving the Past, Shaping the Future
clevelandpark.summary: A 28-minute video narrated by Jim Lehrer that uses interviews with key participants and archival footage to tell how residents organized to protect the neighborhood's historic character and save Rosedale from development.

chevychase.title: A Backward Glance, 1898-1933
chevychase.summary: A speech by the retired principal of the Chevy Chase School, later the E.V. Brown School, which opened in March 1898 on the site of today's community center. She describes a four-room building amid mud and thickets, 25 pupils from outlying farms when only Connecticut Avenue was cut through, and stove-heated classrooms.

chevychase.title: Dallas Dean
chevychase.summary: Dean, who lived from birth in her family's stone house in Chevy Chase, tells how her grandfather bought about 40 acres in the early 1900s, reaching it by streetcar, and how the land was sold after his 1945 death, with houses along Rittenhouse built in the early 1950s.

chevychase.title: Ralph Benson
chevychase.summary: Benson describes his parents finding their house on Upland Terrace by chance during the Depression, the farmland across Western Avenue, and, in the 1940s, Pinehurst Circle neighbors raising money to buy out a racially mixed couple who had bought a house there.

chevychase.title: Samuel Frank Higger and Marie Silverman Higger
chevychase.summary: An oral history prepared around 1999 from an interview with Marie Higger. Sam Higger bought a building in the 5800 block of Connecticut Avenue in 1930 and installed a big soda fountain that became a neighborhood meeting place; the store was the first in the area to carry penicillin. She recalls a warning that some might oppose a Jewish pharmacist.

chevychase.title: Helen Higgins
chevychase.summary: Higgins, a Chevy Chase native and sculptor, lives in what the archive calls the oldest house in Chevy Chase DC. She describes the house her builder father designed in 1925 and his family's earlier years in a shotgun house beside the Broad Branch Market.

chevychase.title: Jean Klieger
chevychase.summary: Klieger, from a German Jewish Washington family, recalls how she and her husband chose Oliver Street in 1956 for Lafayette School, looking for swing sets in back yards, and how glad they were to find a neighborhood without restrictions against Jews. Mothers volunteered heavily at Lafayette.

chevychase.title: Thomas and Mae Scanlan
chevychase.summary: The couple explain why they stayed in the city while others left for the suburbs. Mae chose their short street for its many children and Lafayette School; she recalls friends moving to Maryland when busing began at Deal Junior High.

chevychase.title: Vera Rubin
chevychase.summary: An interview the astronomer gave about the neighborhood rather than her science. Rubin traces her family's moves, coming to Washington, and settling in the Chevy Chase house where she arrived with three children while her husband was still in Illinois; their fourth child came in 1960.

chevychase.title: Allen Beach
chevychase.summary: Beach recalls moving to Chevy Chase Parkway in 1942, hearing about D-Day in 1944, pickup games on Nevada Avenue and at Lafayette, Maryland children crossing Western Avenue to D.C. schools, and the 1942 builder houses on streets such as Rittenhouse and Stuyvesant.

chevychase.title: Milton Kotler
chevychase.summary: Kotler, described by the archive as father of the ANCs and the neighborhood government movement, recounts his Chicago youth, studies and community organizing with Saul Alinsky, and coming to Washington to join a new policy institute based near Dupont Circle.

friendshipheights.title: Frances Hamby
friendshipheights.summary: Hamby recalls gas stations on all four corners of Wisconsin Avenue and Jenifer Street, gas at about 30 cents a gallon, how little shopping there was before Woodward and Lothrop arrived, and the Silver Fox restaurant with a pianist where Mazza Gallerie now stands.

friendshipheights.title: William Gray
friendshipheights.summary: Gray, who remembers Washington as a sleepy Southern town where $1 bought a weekly streetcar pass, mentions a neighbor whose father ran the Silver Fox restaurant on Wisconsin Avenue, where shops were leveled for Mazza Gallerie, and a local collection of streetcar photographs.

friendshipheights.title: Patty Myler
friendshipheights.summary: Myler recalls that going out to dinner was a big event for her parents, who sometimes chose the Silver Fox, a restaurant where Mazza Gallerie now stands, along with neighborhood stores such as Broad Branch Market and Brookville Market.

capitolhill.title: George Hutchinson
capitolhill.summary: Hutchinson grew up around Stanton Park and lived there until just after World War II. He recalls serving as a Supreme Court page in knickers, its tunnels, night school across town, and later work in the Court's library and Marshal's Office, along with neighborhood schools, movies, ice cream parlors, trolleys, Lindbergh's return and the Bonus Marchers.
capitolhill.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

capitolhill.title: Tony Ambrosi
capitolhill.summary: Born in 1911, Ambrosi grew up in Schott's Place, an Italian enclave inside the block now occupied by the Dirksen and Hart Senate buildings, where children played ball on the Belgian-block courtyard. Interviewed by his grandson, he recalls playing inside the Capitol dome, meeting the Army the day the Bonus Marchers were routed, and finishing cement on the Federal Triangle.
capitolhill.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

capitolhill.title: Helene Au
capitolhill.summary: Born on Capitol Hill, Au lived nearly all of her 105 years there; her German immigrant grandfather settled on the Hill in 1873 to play in the Marine Band. She describes early 20th-century life: an inventor uncle working from the family carriage house, corner stores, movie theaters, games, schools, World War I, and driving early cars.
capitolhill.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

capitolhill.title: Goldie Mamakos
capitolhill.summary: Born on the Hill in 1930 into a Greek immigrant household, Mamakos describes relatives who ran Club Kavakos, a candy store, Richfield Dairy and Sherrill's Bakery. She remembers checking coats at Club Kavakos, Friendship House, and the Marion Park police precinct where boys played ping pong and children got Christmas stockings. Includes family and Wallach School photos.
capitolhill.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

capitolhill.title: Esther Woodfolk
capitolhill.summary: The houses where Woodfolk grew up were demolished for the Southeast-Southwest Freeway, but she remembers her Depression-era neighborhood well: programs at the Southeast Settlement House, her hard-working father, the Southeast library, and everyday scenes of the Black community in the 1930s and 1940s.
capitolhill.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

capitolhill.title: Lloyd Thompson
capitolhill.summary: Thompson's family came to the 1300 block of East Capitol Street in the mid-1950s after being displaced by what he calls 'urban removal' in Southwest. He recalls families on his block, local businesses, churches, theaters, old streetcar lines, buses and the arrival of Metro, plus his later work as a cowboy out West.
capitolhill.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

capitolhill.title: Hazel Kreinheder
capitolhill.summary: Kreinheder and her husband bought a house on Kentucky Avenue just off Lincoln Park in 1963. In 1974 she and Ruth Ann Overbeck interviewed longtime residents for the historic district application, recordings she later gave to the project. Her 2015-16 interviews cover Hill life, local businesses, neighbors and events, especially around her own block.
capitolhill.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

capitolhill.title: Larry Monaco
capitolhill.summary: Monaco spent his early childhood on the Hill, as his parents had, before his family moved to Prince George's County in the late 1940s. He returned in 1967 and twice led the Capitol Hill Restoration Society. He recalls corner stores, snow cones, barbershops, shoe repair shops and an Italian uncle's businesses on New Jersey Avenue SE.
capitolhill.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

capitolhill.title: Hattie McLaurin
capitolhill.summary: McLaurin moved from a North Carolina farm in 1956, trained as a practical nurse, and spent over 30 years as a nanny for Capitol Hill families, which made her an expert on local shops, libraries, Eastern Market and the parks. She discusses daily Hill life and events from the 1968 riots to the 2018 Arthur Capper senior housing fire.
capitolhill.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

capitolhill.title: Mike Bowers
capitolhill.summary: Bowers's family has run Bowers Fancy Dairy Products in Eastern Market since his grandfather bought it from the Sweeney family in 1964. He talks about changes in the market and the dairy trade, cheeses and customers, and family stories reaching back through the Civil War, the B&O Railroad, Union Station and the White House.
capitolhill.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

hstreet.title: Anwar Saleem
hstreet.summary: Saleem was a teenager when the 1968 riots wrecked H Street NE, where he had bought his first jeans at McBride's and found his first job. Decades later he led the H Street Merchants Association and then H Street Main Street, and here he describes the joint effort by officials, developers, businesses and residents to bring the corridor back.
hstreet.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

hstreet.title: Sidney Hoffman
hstreet.summary: Hoffman spent his earliest years living above his father's shoe store on H Street NE and moved around Northeast and Southeast in the 1920s. After Eastern High School (class of 1937) he managed theaters, meeting stars of the day and once shaking hands with Franklin Roosevelt, before becoming a gemologist.
hstreet.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

hstreet.title: Jean Noel
hstreet.summary: Born on F Street NE, Noel recalls her childhood in the neighborhood near H Street NE: its shops and theaters, alley dwellings without plumbing or electricity, Ludlow and Taylor schools, Stuart Junior High and Eastern High. Other memories include skating around the Supreme Court site and people-watching from behind the statues at Union Station.
hstreet.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

hstreet.title: Adele Robey
hstreet.summary: Robey and her husband Bruce worked on early efforts to develop the Atlas Theater on H Street NE, then founded the H Street Playhouse (2001-2012) and published the Voice of the Hill newspaper (1999-2010). She traces the growth of community and professional theater on Capitol Hill and beyond, including her later work with the Anacostia Playhouse.
hstreet.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

hstreet.title: Jane Lang
hstreet.summary: Lawyer and philanthropist Lang led the effort that turned the long-abandoned Atlas movie house on H Street NE into the Atlas Performing Arts Center, which since 2006 has hosted theater, dance, music and children's programs. Recorded when she received a 2024 Capitol Hill Community Achievement Award.
hstreet.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

hstreet.title: H Street Oral History Project
hstreet.summary: Mosaic Theater Company, based on H Street NE, interviewed past and present corridor residents about the 1968 riots and the 2020 protests, and playwrights turned the interviews into new plays staged at a 2024 festival. DCist reported that audio of the monologues would be preserved in DC Public Library's archives.
hstreet.archive: Mosaic Theater Company (recordings to be deposited with DC Public Library)

navyyard.title: Michael Shiner diary (his "book"), 1813-1860s
navyyard.summary: Shiner, born enslaved in 1805, was leased to the Navy Yard paint shop in 1828 and worked there most of his life, later as a free man. His journal opens with the British invasion and burning of the Capitol and Navy Yard, then follows Yard working conditions, the city's racial tensions and military and civilian life. The manuscript is held by the Library of Congress.
navyyard.archive: Library of Congress (Manuscript Division; exhibition biography)

navyyard.title: Carolyn Mitchell interview, 2017-08-07
navyyard.summary: Mitchell, who came from Detroit in 2004 and works for the American Society of Landscape Architects, talks about helping shape community-led plans for Southwest. She describes frustration that officials set aside residents' plans in favor of projects she feels hurt people living near the Buzzard Point industrial area. Part of the Buzzard Point Oral History Project.
navyyard.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (Buzzard Point Oral History Project, DC Oral History Collaborative)

anacostia.title: Raymond Henderson interview, 2018-07-02
anacostia.summary: Born in 1948, Henderson spent most of his childhood in Anacostia, left high school in 1966 to join the Marines and fight in Vietnam, then enrolled at Federal City College, where he helped form the Black Leopards student group. He also discusses student journalism, a trip to Cuba, PTSD and addiction, and his career as a photographer.
anacostia.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative)

anacostia.title: Daniel T. Brooking interview, 2024-11-13
anacostia.summary: The photographer and digital artist describes growing up in Anacostia and attending Anacostia High School as DC schools integrated, where art teacher Phillip Ratner shaped his path. He also talks about 33 years at the Agriculture Department, art classes at American University and Federal City College, and joining Black Artists of D.C.
anacostia.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative)

anacostia.title: Arrington Dixon interview, 2017-11-19
anacostia.summary: The former DC councilmember recalls growing up in Anacostia, segregation and discrimination, the church's place in his life, riding trolleys to McKinley High School, his brother's death, and moving to Lamond Riggs while at Howard University. Recorded for the Desegregation in Ward 4 project.
anacostia.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative)

anacostia.title: Kenneth Carroll interview, 2022-05-01
anacostia.summary: The poet talks about growing up, becoming a writer, and creating 8Rock, an arts space and open mic series based in Anacostia, plus his work with DC WritersCorps and the growth of a writers' community the archive calls unique to the city.
anacostia.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative)

anacostia.title: Mildred Raby interview, 2023-10-10
anacostia.summary: Born in 1926, Raby moved to Anacostia in 1937 and soon into Barry Farm Dwellings, her community for roughly five decades. She recalls school and social life under segregation, local businesses, Campbell AME Church and her years as an educator there, before rising violence led her to move to Virginia in the 1980s.
anacostia.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative)

anacostia.title: Helen Thompson interview, 2023-06-13
anacostia.summary: Thompson's family moved from Charlottesville to Barry Farm Dwellings in 1943. She describes the community built by neighbors, organizers and churchgoers, and helping integrate Anacostia High School, which she compares with what her own children later faced in Montgomery County schools.
anacostia.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative)

anacostia.title: Emory Foster interview, 2023-07-18
anacostia.summary: Born on Sheridan Road in 1930 to parents from Anacostia, Foster recalls a Barry Farm childhood centered on the recreation center, church and local businesses, schools in three quadrants, and a working life that ran from Qualls Pharmacy to 39 years with the DC Recreation Department.
anacostia.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative)

anacostia.title: Deborah Boston interview, 2023-07-25
anacostia.summary: Boston's family moved to Barry Farm Dwellings in 1957. She describes neighbors who shared what they had, 1950s youth life, school before and after desegregation, thriving local businesses, the toll eminent domain took on Barry Farm and Anacostia residents, and Campbell AME Church.
anacostia.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative)

anacostia.title: Joyce Bond interview, 2023-08-08
anacostia.summary: Bond came to Barry Farm Dwellings in 1943 and grew up in a strict household run by her mother and aunt. She talks about Campbell AME Church and the love of singing it fostered, and segregated DC schools including Birney, Randall and Dunbar, before marrying and moving elsewhere in the city in 1953.
anacostia.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative)

anacostia.title: Alyce Burke interview, 2023-06-27
anacostia.summary: Burke moved to Barry Farm from Virginia at age three. She recalls a childhood centered on the recreation center run by Florence Matthews and Stanley Anderson, local businesses and churches, segregated schools, and the income limits that made her family leave Barry Farm for 4th Street NE.
anacostia.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative)

brookland.title: Robert Malesky interview, 2023-08-16
brookland.summary: The author of the Bygone Brookland blog describes coming to DC for Catholic University, his NPR career and how Brookland has changed since 1970. He also shares findings from his research: Black and white migration, the Old Soldiers' Home, transit, land claims older than the Civil War, and highways once proposed through the neighborhood.

brookland.title: Barbara Currie interview, 2021-08-12
brookland.summary: Currie grew up in LeDroit Park and moved with her family to Brookland in 1962, where she had close white friends even as some of their parents discriminated against her. She recalls Slowe Elementary in Brookland, being stranded at Glen Echo Park in 1966, the 1968 protests after King's assassination, and decades as a nurse.
brookland.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative)

brookland.title: Felicia Jones interview, 2021-06-28
brookland.summary: A native Washingtonian who has worked for the Edgewood/Brookland Family Support Collaborative since it began in the late 1990s, and was one of its original employees hired from the Brookland neighborhood, talks about growing up in DC, a stay in North Carolina, and more than 20 years with the organization.
brookland.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative)

brookland.title: Carla Perlo interview
brookland.summary: The co-founder and longtime director of Dance Place reflects on building it into a presenter, school and community arts center in Ward 5's Brookland/Edgewood area over 40 years, how the DanceAfrica, DC festival fits that history, her legacy, and the future of dance after COVID-19.
brookland.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative)

brookland.title: The Brookland Literary And Hunting Club (BLAHC): It's Not What You Think!
brookland.summary: Six interviews recorded in 2018 with the last five members of the Brookland Literary and Hunting Club and one spouse. Nine Black professionals, many tied to Howard University, founded the invitation-only club in Brookland in 1942; for more than 75 years members met monthly to discuss the issues of the day and play poker.
brookland.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative)

brookland.title: James Butts interview, 2018-04-20
brookland.summary: A longtime social worker whom three DC mayors appointed to run a city department talks about public service, college in segregated Alabama, a Howard University social work degree, work with SNCC and helping found the RFK Foundation. He also stresses the literary side of the Brookland Literary and Hunting Club.
brookland.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative)

brookland.title: Walter K. Robinson interview, 2018-04-18
brookland.summary: Born in Baltimore in 1920, Robinson recalls leaving Howard University for the Army Air Corps in 1941 and becoming a Tuskegee Airman, a career at the post office in DC, and segregation and desegregation. For decades, the archive notes, the Brookland Literary and Hunting Club was where he went for relaxation and companionship.
brookland.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative)

brookland.title: Jock Banks interview, 2018-06-19
brookland.summary: Born in 1953 and one of the club's younger members, Banks, a lawyer and the son of a doctor and a teacher who both played poker, followed his father into the Brookland Literary and Hunting Club. He talks about white flight, the later return of white residents, and the history and decline of the club's poker group.
brookland.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative)

brookland.title: BLAHC Reflections: Women Take a Seat at the Table
brookland.summary: A 2022 extension of the club's oral history project, created with All Souls Church, records women whose lives touched the men of the Brookland Literary and Hunting Club, which ended in 2019. They tell their own stories, talk about card games as a source of friendship through segregation and the pandemic, and add memories of the club.
brookland.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative)

noma.title: Florine Jones interview, 1992-11-03
noma.summary: Recorded for the St. Mary's Court Oral History Project. The archive describes Jones as a third-generation Washingtonian raised in Shaw who later lived with her husband and children in the area now called NoMa. She worked at the Pentagon and for 15 years at the Air and Space Museum. Two audio parts and a transcript.
noma.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (St. Mary's Court Oral History Project)

noma.title: Florince remembers major events at the Washington Coliseum/Uline Arena
noma.summary: A short clip filed under Ward 6. The page notes that the arena opened in 1941, anchored the neighborhood's cultural life, and drew local families and national acts. Jones recalls the excitement of growing up a few blocks from it.
noma.archive: hometown DC (HumanitiesDC, DC Oral History Collaborative)

noma.title: Raymond Coates interview, 2021-08-19
noma.summary: A former staff member of the Edgewood/Brookland Family Support Collaborative traces his work back to the early Collaborative movement, starting with the North Capitol Collaborative. The archive says Coates, a native Washingtonian, was raised in the NoMa neighborhood, specifically the H Street corridor. Audio, index and transcript.
noma.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (HumanitiesDC, DC Oral History Collaborative)

noma.title: Richard Crayton interview, 2024-05-18
noma.summary: Crayton, whose family settled in DC in the mid-1950s, recalls skating during segregation. He does not remember any city rink that admitted Black skaters, so he and his friends skated at Sherwood Recreation Center and on Black Saturday at Uline Arena. He later became a skate DJ at the National Roller Arena on Kalorama Road.
noma.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (HumanitiesDC, DC Oral History Collaborative)

lenfantplaza.title: John Lucas interview, 1983-03-19
lenfantplaza.summary: Lucas, born in Southwest in 1885, describes community life in his youth: farms, housing, the cost of living, segregation, entertainment and crime. He also covers what he saw during urban renewal, including businesses relocating, better living conditions and new roads and transit. Recorded for Dolores Smith's film project 'Southwest Remembered.'
lenfantplaza.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library ('Southwest Remembered: A Story of Urban Renewal' Oral History Project)

lenfantplaza.title: Mignon Coates interview, 1983-06-18
lenfantplaza.summary: Coates, born and raised in Southwest, remembers the neighborhood before urban renewal: its schools and businesses, the talent among the people she grew up with, and the central place of church. Urban renewal forced her out and separated her from loved ones.
lenfantplaza.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library ('Southwest Remembered: A Story of Urban Renewal' Oral History Project)

lenfantplaza.title: Mr. and Mrs. Walter Butler interview, 1983-06-12
lenfantplaza.summary: The Butlers, former Southwest residents, recall the community before urban renewal: recreation, living conditions, schools, clubs and businesses from their childhood, and misconceptions about the area. Many residents could not return after redevelopment, so former neighbors keep in touch through reunion picnics.
lenfantplaza.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library ('Southwest Remembered: A Story of Urban Renewal' Oral History Project)

lenfantplaza.title: Mary Jefferson interview, 1983-02-20
lenfantplaza.summary: Jefferson draws on her years in show business to recall musicians and dancers she knew in Southwest and the neighborhood's club and hall scene. She also describes how urban renewal wiped out livelihoods and broke the relationships that had helped the community get by.
lenfantplaza.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library ('Southwest Remembered: A Story of Urban Renewal' Oral History Project)

lenfantplaza.title: Betty Shapiro interview, 1983-05-13
lenfantplaza.summary: Shapiro describes growing up in the largely Jewish part of Southwest, a hard-working, close community, until she left the city at 14. She also talks about other Jewish communities around DC, the area's few amenities before urban renewal, and the arrival of white and Black newcomers.
lenfantplaza.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library ('Southwest Remembered: A Story of Urban Renewal' Oral History Project)

lenfantplaza.title: Reverend Norman Haddad interview, 1983-02-24
lenfantplaza.summary: Father Haddad, a priest at St. Dominic Church, talks about Southwest's places of worship before urban renewal and residents' joint efforts to save the community they had built. He says churches and parks gave the neighborhood a family feeling that faded after redevelopment.
lenfantplaza.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library ('Southwest Remembered: A Story of Urban Renewal' Oral History Project)

lenfantplaza.title: James Banks interview, 1984-11-29
lenfantplaza.summary: Banks, former Director of Relocation for the Redevelopment Land Agency, talks about the families he moved during Southwest's urban renewal, his job of placing them in new housing, the problems he ran into, his conversations with residents, and the costs and benefits of the redevelopment.
lenfantplaza.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library ('Southwest Remembered: A Story of Urban Renewal' Oral History Project)

lenfantplaza.title: Morris Engle interview, 1985-04-14
lenfantplaza.summary: Engle, former owner of the Southwest restaurant Harrigan's, describes his unsuccessful efforts to save small family businesses during urban renewal and his dealings with officials who could have helped displaced owners. He also tells stories of racial integration in the neighborhood.
lenfantplaza.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library ('Southwest Remembered: A Story of Urban Renewal' Oral History Project)

lenfantplaza.title: Vanessa Ruffin-Colbert interview, 2017-08-22
lenfantplaza.summary: Ruffin-Colbert, a native Washingtonian who has spent much of her life in the Southwest home where she was born, talks about her community work with local children and families, neighborhood problems, redevelopment and construction, and her role connecting residents with public officials. She is also passionate about the arts.
lenfantplaza.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (Buzzard Point Oral History Project, DC Oral History Collaborative)

lenfantplaza.title: Thelma D. Jones interview, 2017-09-26
lenfantplaza.summary: Jones talks about moving to Washington and living in Southwest, the World Bank's summer jobs program for youth, the history of the Southwest Neighborhood Assembly and her work on its task forces, the Southwest Neighborhood Small Area Plan, the breast cancer fund she founded, and changes in the neighborhood.
lenfantplaza.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (Buzzard Point Oral History Project, DC Oral History Collaborative)

palisades.title: History of the Palisades Community Association
palisades.summary: A community history written for the association's 40th anniversary in 1956 and updated for its 50th in 1966, drawing on old families' memories: the Weaver, Sherier and Boyle farms, soldiers from Battery Kemble raiding a farmhouse, freed families given land on Chain Bridge Road, and descendants still living locally in the 1960s.
palisades.archive: Palisades Community Association (founded 1916 as the Conduit Road Citizens Association)

columbiaheights.title: Apolonia Lopez interview, 2022-10-02
columbiaheights.summary: A second-generation resident of Urban Village, an affordable complex on Newton Street, and vice president of its tenant association recalls growing up there and the residents' recent sale to a new developer under DC's tenant purchase law, including the building's roots in St. Stephen's Church's reparations to the Black community.
columbiaheights.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative: Newton Street/The Cooperative at 1477 and Black Women Warriors)

columbiaheights.title: Bill MacKaye interview, 2022-07-12
columbiaheights.summary: A St. Stephen's Church leader since 1962 recalls how the congregation, recruited as one of DC's first integrated Episcopal churches, became an affordable housing developer on Newton Street in response to the Black Power movement's call for reparations, and his decades working with Black and Latino housing activists, many of them women.
columbiaheights.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative: Newton Street/The Cooperative at 1477 and Black Women Warriors)

columbiaheights.title: Renee Flood Wright interview, 2022-07-11
columbiaheights.summary: A DC-born artist and teacher who moved from a house in Mount Pleasant to an apartment on Newton Street describes twenty years as a leader at Urban Village and the unusual partnership that will let longtime residents share in the building's ownership and cash-flow profits.
columbiaheights.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative: Newton Street/The Cooperative at 1477 and Black Women Warriors)

columbiaheights.title: Marlene Manzo interview, 2022-07-25
columbiaheights.summary: The first board president of The Cooperative at 1477, a limited-equity cooperative converted from a tax-credit rental on Newton Street, connects her childhood among Mexican migrant farmworkers in Washington state to the work of turning a diverse building of renters into co-owners.
columbiaheights.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative: Newton Street/The Cooperative at 1477 and Black Women Warriors)

columbiaheights.title: Teresa Edmondson interview part 1, 2022-05-23
columbiaheights.summary: A community activist recounts three decades of work that ended with her rental building converted into a limited-equity housing cooperative, honoring its purpose as a home for people recovering from substance abuse, and the family lessons about homeownership that shaped her.
columbiaheights.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative: Newton Street/The Cooperative at 1477 and Black Women Warriors)

columbiaheights.title: Columbia Heights Day 2023
columbiaheights.summary: Archive collection of oral history recordings and transcripts the Humanities Truck gathered at Columbia Heights Day on June 24, 2023, along with photographs of the event.
columbiaheights.archive: Humanities Truck Community Archive, American University Archives

columbiaheights.title: Marita Golden interview, 2014
columbiaheights.summary: The novelist recalls a childhood in Columbia Heights and Foggy Bottom, covering the riot-damaged U Street corridor as a freshman reporter for American University's paper, and becoming a community activist afterward, volunteering for Marion Barry's Pride Inc. and the Freedom School.
columbiaheights.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (U Street Oral History Project)

ustreet.title: Alva Lorena Smith Marcus interview, 2014
ustreet.summary: She grew up in the U Street corridor, where her father owned or managed several businesses, drove a cab and ran messages for the FBI. She describes community, childhood and her years at Howard, and the corridor's shift toward more Black-owned businesses.
ustreet.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (U Street Oral History Project)

ustreet.title: C. Bernard Ruffin interview, part 1 of 3, 2014
ustreet.summary: A DC-born writer recalls a childhood in the U Street area, where his father was a beat officer and a leader of the local Police Boys' Club and his aunts taught at a nearby high school, along with segregation and how the community changed over his lifetime.
ustreet.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (U Street Oral History Project)

ustreet.title: James A. Bennett interview, part 1 of 2, 2014
ustreet.summary: Bennett grew up in the U Street corridor and describes understanding segregation as a child, performing on the street as a boy, and later going to the area's clubs and theaters, tracing how the community changed as he grew up.
ustreet.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (U Street Oral History Project)

ustreet.title: Gregory Lamont Gaskins interview, 2014
ustreet.summary: A self-taught guitarist who toured with the Manhattans and Elvis Presley describes the clubs along 14th Street in the U Street corridor from his childhood and the famous groups that came through town.
ustreet.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (U Street Oral History Project)

ustreet.title: James Elias Smoot interview, 2014
ustreet.summary: As a teenager Smoot ushered and ran errands for touring bands at the Howard Theatre, meeting many groups he admired. He recalls the night of the 1968 riots, when a 14th Street club canceled his band's show and the band joined the looting.
ustreet.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (U Street Oral History Project)

ustreet.title: Sandra Butler-Truesdale interview, 2014
ustreet.summary: She grew up in the U Street corridor in a family of civil rights activists, graduated from Cardozo and Howard, built youth music programs for the District, and later worked as a cosmetologist for James Brown. She traces the corridor's changing character.
ustreet.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (U Street Oral History Project)

ustreet.title: Alice Gail Pollard Clark interview, 2021-10-23
ustreet.summary: Clark describes her family history and childhood in LeDroit Park, her teachers and school traditions such as May Day at Mott Elementary, and her path to Howard, Catholic University and law school; in 1997 she became Howard County, Maryland's first Black judge.
ustreet.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative: Stories of the Mott School in LeDroit Park)

ustreet.title: Barbara Currie interview, 2021-08-12
ustreet.summary: Currie grew up on Oakdale Place in LeDroit Park and attended Lucretia Mott Elementary from 1956 to 1962. She recalls her family's 1962 move to Brookland, being stranded at Glen Echo in 1966 after a race-related fight, the 1968 protests, and nursing through the AIDS crisis.
ustreet.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative: Stories of the Mott School in LeDroit Park)

ustreet.title: Charlene Drew Jarvis interview, 2021-09-13
ustreet.summary: The scientist and former Ward 4 councilmember grew up in LeDroit Park and describes the supportive community her family found at Howard and the Mott School, losing her father, blood-transfusion pioneer Dr. Charles Drew, in a car accident, and segregation and integration in DC schools.
ustreet.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative: Stories of the Mott School in LeDroit Park)

ustreet.title: Elinor Craig Taylor interview, 2021-08-25
ustreet.summary: Born in LeDroit Park in 1932, Taylor attended Mott School through sixth grade. She remembers her house and the neighborhood's stores, her father's work as a Pullman porter, and later teaching at Shaw Junior High School.
ustreet.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative: Stories of the Mott School in LeDroit Park)

shaw.title: Barbara Taylor Hunter interview, part 1, April 2012
shaw.summary: Hunter describes the fashion and culture of Shaw and Howard in the 1960s, campus political groups and the music scene, and how the 1968 riots changed the neighborhood: lost buildings, departing families and rising housing costs. A former teacher, she also talks about Shaw's schools.
shaw.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (South of U Oral History Project)

shaw.title: Yvonne Baskerville interview, April 2012
shaw.summary: Baskerville discusses her schooling at Dunbar, the segregated Black high school, her shock at the news of Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination, and her run-ins with the city's rats.
shaw.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (South of U Oral History Project)

shaw.title: Kenneth Tolliver interview, April 2012
shaw.summary: A DC native compares the 1968 riots to a battle scene, notes that many destroyed businesses never came back, and sees gentrification as an issue Shaw has faced ever since. He also talks about Fides House, a neighborhood community center.
shaw.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (South of U Oral History Project)

shaw.title: Mill Butler interview, April 2012
shaw.summary: Butler describes going out to the Howard and Republic theaters and explains how car dealerships left the neighborhood after the 1968 riots because they could no longer get insurance.
shaw.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (South of U Oral History Project)

shaw.title: Jacqueline Rogers Hart interview, April 2012
shaw.summary: Born in Washington, Hart returned from fashion school in New York to work as a secretary and was at a law firm when the 1968 riots broke out. She reflects on how Shaw has changed, costing more and no longer as close-knit as it was.
shaw.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (South of U Oral History Project)

shaw.title: Ibrahim Mumin interview, June 2012
shaw.summary: Mumin recalls student activism at Howard that pushed the university toward the community and drew him to Shaw, Fides House, and the clubs and restaurants he frequented. He reflects on why the 1968 riots happened, the flight of businesses and middle-class whites, and Shaw's economic and cultural future.
shaw.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (South of U Oral History Project)

shaw.title: Elizabeth Williams Frazier interview, April 2012
shaw.summary: Frazier moved to Shaw as a child in 1963 and attended Shaw Junior High. She remembers a close-knit community where everyone knew each other, Fides House as a place for food and clothing, hearing of King's assassination, and blocks that stayed in ruins for years after the riots.
shaw.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (South of U Oral History Project)

shaw.title: Karen Keegan-Isard interview, part 1, May 2012
shaw.summary: Keegan-Isard describes moving to Washington with her husband and eventually to Shaw, the community bank he founded in the neighborhood, and her experience of the 1968 riots.
shaw.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (South of U Oral History Project)

shaw.title: Alexander Padro interview, June 2012
shaw.summary: A longtime Shaw organizer reflects on the causes and effects of the 1968 riots and on urban renewal led by churches and large housing projects rather than businesses, including disputes between community groups and the redevelopment agency. He also touches on the crack epidemic.
shaw.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (South of U Oral History Project)

shaw.title: Betty May Brooks-Cole interview, May 2012
shaw.summary: Brooks-Cole describes U Street's entertainment venues for Black Washingtonians, including the Howard and Republic theaters and acts such as Chuck Brown and the Four Tops, segregated department stores, and her fright at being on 7th Street in the middle of the 1968 riots.
shaw.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (South of U Oral History Project)

logancircle.title: Oral History with Maurice Dorsey (LCCA), 2022-06-15
logancircle.summary: A thirty-year Logan Circle resident, author and former ANC commissioner recalls a quiet life with two long-term partners and a 1990s divide between tree-lined 15th Street and a 14th Street marked by drugs, crime and prostitution, when Annie's on 17th Street and bars like Friends and Halo were safe places.
logancircle.archive: Rainbow History Project Digital Collections (with the Logan Circle Community Association and the Washington Blade)

logancircle.title: Oral History with Ed Bailey (LCCA), 2022-06-04
logancircle.summary: Bailey, who grew up in DC, moved to Logan Circle in 1994. He recalls avoiding the circle itself, friends who wouldn't visit when there were no amenities, and the change as gay life migrated from Dupont Circle and new shops, restaurants and, in 2002, the bar Halo arrived.
logancircle.archive: Rainbow History Project Digital Collections (with the Logan Circle Community Association and the Washington Blade)

logancircle.title: Oral History with Marc Fallow and Larry Rosen (LCCA), 2022-06-16
logancircle.summary: Two men who moved to Logan Circle in 1980 and 1981 and shared a group house found through ads at Lambda Rising and in the Washington Blade. They recall a neighborhood in flux, with little dining or shopping, treks to gay spots elsewhere in the city, gay choruses and activism.
logancircle.archive: Rainbow History Project Digital Collections (with the Logan Circle Community Association and the Washington Blade)

logancircle.title: Oral History with John Guggenmos (LCCA), 2022-06-17
logancircle.summary: Guggenmos came from Wyoming in 1989 for college and took a cheap group-house room at Logan Circle, east of what he calls the 'magic line' of 15th Street. A later ANC member and bar and restaurant owner, he covers gay life moving east from Dupont, Pride's evolution, real estate and safety.
logancircle.archive: Rainbow History Project Digital Collections (with the Logan Circle Community Association and the Washington Blade)

logancircle.title: Oral History with Sak Pollert (LCCA), 2022-06-06
logancircle.summary: A Thai immigrant who arrived in 1991 and found community through Asian and Friends recalls 16th Street as the line between safe and unsafe streets, the close circle of 1990s merchants on 14th Street, opening his restaurant Rice in 2003, and how apps changed what a 'gay neighborhood' means.
logancircle.archive: Rainbow History Project Digital Collections (with the Logan Circle Community Association and the Washington Blade)

logancircle.title: Oral History with Nicolas Shi (LCCA), 2022-06-22
logancircle.summary: An artist from El Salvador who bought a Logan Circle house in 1988 describes the artists' studios around 14th Street, founding MidCity Artists' open studios, parties that moved on to gay bars, friends too afraid of crime to visit, and the 'walking blocks' and 'running blocks' east of 15th Street.
logancircle.archive: Rainbow History Project Digital Collections (with the Logan Circle Community Association and the Washington Blade)

logancircle.title: Oral History with Jeff Travers (LCCA), 2022-06-14
logancircle.summary: Hired at Whitman-Walker Clinic in 1991, Travers recalls its supportive housing for people with AIDS, serving as an ANC commissioner amid conflicts such as opposition to a new N Street Village facility, and buying a condominium in a Vermont Avenue mansion in 1992.
logancircle.archive: Rainbow History Project Digital Collections (with the Logan Circle Community Association and the Washington Blade)

chinatown.title: Harry Lee Chow interview, 2019-06-30
chinatown.summary: Chow grew up in the 1950s on North Capitol Street, a mile from Chinatown, where his father ran a laundry. He recalls Lady Bird Johnson's beautification work in Chinatown, the Chinatown Courtesy Patrol and Creative Workshop, working at Chinatown Tropicals, the 1968 riots, and changes brought by gentrification.
chinatown.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative: Chinatown Voices)

chinatown.title: Jack Lee interview, 2019-07-27
chinatown.summary: Born in 1953 to immigrants from Taishan, Lee grew up in the center of Chinatown above his father's grocery. He recalls the Lee Family Association, a youth program he ran in Chinatown in 1971, school in a mostly Black neighborhood, and the decline that began with the convention center and arena.
chinatown.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative: Chinatown Voices)

chinatown.title: Mei interview, 2019-09-21
chinatown.summary: Mei came from Hong Kong at age 7 and lived near Chinatown. She talks about other Chinatown kids, the Chinatown program at Calvary Baptist Church, helping at her grandfather's laundry, Chinese holidays, and her belief that another Chinatown could spring up elsewhere.
chinatown.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative: Chinatown Voices)

chinatown.title: Sunny Luk interview, 2019-09-28
chinatown.summary: Luk came from Hong Kong at 5 and helped make noodles at his father's Chinatown restaurant. He discusses relations between Chinese and Black residents, children's programs in Chinatown including the Chinese Young Club, and generational differences between immigrants and their children.
chinatown.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative: Chinatown Voices)

chinatown.title: Wallace Lee interview, 2019-09-16
chinatown.summary: Lee came from Hong Kong as a baby and grew up above his father's laundry. He recalls the Lee Family Association, sports with other Chinatown kids, the family's move to the suburbs, and the decline of DC's Chinatown, which he hopes to see preserved.
chinatown.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative: Chinatown Voices)

bloomingdale.title: David Nicholson interview, 2017
bloomingdale.summary: Writer and former journalist Nicholson moved in with his grandparents in Bloomingdale in 1960, when his mother returned to D.C. from Jamaica. In three parts he talks about growing up there, DC public schools, being among the small group of Black students who integrated Sidwell Friends, and his family's church.

bloomingdale.title: Tony Norman interview, 2023
bloomingdale.summary: Norman came to D.C. in 1984 for law school at Howard and stayed on as a civic activist and attorney. He covers lawsuits against the city and federal governments over development, including an unbuilt prison near McMillan Reservoir, and work to preserve the historic sites at McMillan.

foggybottom.title: Oral History Interview with Mary Brown
foggybottom.summary: Brown was born in Foggy Bottom in 1920, and the association lists her as a resident since the 1920s. Laetitia Combrinck interviewed her at GWU's Gelman Library for the university's oral history program.
foggybottom.archive: Foggy Bottom Association History Project (GWU Oral History Program)

foggybottom.title: Oral History Interview with Eric Marlow
foggybottom.summary: Marlow calls his memories of a Foggy Bottom childhood in the 1950s bittersweet: the neighborhood was physically segregated, he says, but its people came together across that line. Part of GWU's oral history program.
foggybottom.archive: Foggy Bottom Association History Project (GWU Oral History Program)

foggybottom.title: James Briscoe and W. David Riley interview
foggybottom.summary: Katie Mead and Bernard Demczuk talk with two former residents about Foggy Bottom in the 1950s and 1960s, starting with the Old Georgetown-Foggy Bottom Reunion that former residents hold at Francis Field each summer.

foggybottom.title: Colbert King interview
foggybottom.summary: Pulitzer Prize-winning Washington Post columnist King talks with Frank Leone for the association's history project and Foggy Bottom West End Village, mainly about the 1940s and 1950s, when Foggy Bottom was majority African American.

foggybottom.title: GWU's Neighborhood panel
foggybottom.who: Colbert King, Mary Brown, W. David Riley, James Briscoe
foggybottom.summary: A February 2012 panel at which King, Brown, Riley and Briscoe traded memories of growing up in Foggy Bottom. Linked from the association's oral history page.

foggybottom.title: Wallace Lee interview, 2019
foggybottom.summary: Lee emigrated from Hong Kong as an infant and grew up above his father's laundry on Pennsylvania Avenue, attending Stevens Elementary. The interview also covers the Lee Family Association and Chinatown's decline. Tagged to the West End and Chinatown.

foggybottom.title: Phylicia Fauntleroy Bowman interview, 2017
foggybottom.summary: Bowman, born in 1947, spent her first years near Washington Circle before her family moved to Brightwood when she was about six. She covers her family history, D.C. public schools during desegregation and the changes on her later block.

foggybottom.title: Bill Jones interview, 2020
foggybottom.summary: Jones talks about his father Parker's career at the Chr. Heurich Brewing Co. from the 1930s to the 1950s: the ice house, the delivery trucks, Christian Heurich's firecrackers, and Parker's work as comptroller. The Foggy Bottom Association lists these Home/Brewed recordings among its oral histories.

hilleast.title: Hazel Kreinheder
hilleast.summary: Kreinheder and her husband bought a house on Kentucky Avenue in 1963 and still lived there in 2020. She interviewed longtime residents for the Capitol Hill Restoration Society in 1974. Her own 2015 and 2016 interviews lean on the blocks closest to her home.
hilleast.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

hilleast.title: Lane Parsons
hilleast.summary: Done for the Barney Circle Neighborhood Watch Association's history effort. Parsons watched G Street SE rowhouses go up in the 1920s, basements dug by horse-drawn plows. He also recalls school, the Bonus Army in the neighborhood and John Philip Sousa's funeral.
hilleast.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

hilleast.title: Ann Higgins
hilleast.summary: Higgins moved to Burke Street SE at age three. When her family left during the block-busting of the 1950s, she commuted back to finish at Eastern. She recalls Bryan School and Eastern, living near the D.C. Jail, wartime Washington and local hospitals.
hilleast.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

hilleast.title: Josephine Shore
hilleast.summary: Born at home in 1919 on H Street SE, Shore spent her first 21 years there. She remembers playing barefoot after summer rains, the corner store, the Italian stonecutter who carved headstones for Congressional Cemetery and the family Model T.
hilleast.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

hilleast.title: Rose Lovelace
hilleast.summary: Josephine Shore's sister grew up on H Street SE near Congressional Cemetery just after World War I. She remembers caring for her younger siblings, hansom cabs and the cars that replaced them, and her school and working days.
hilleast.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

hilleast.title: Albert Turner
hilleast.summary: Born in Southeast in 1928, Turner spent most of his childhood on G Street SE. He recalls the paving of cobblestone streets in 1939, delivering groceries to the Marine Commandant's house and living without indoor plumbing, then a career with the telephone company and Capitol Police.
hilleast.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

hilleast.title: Isaac Fulwood, Jr.
hilleast.summary: Before he was D.C. police chief from 1989 to 1992, Fulwood grew up near Kentucky Avenue SE. In two interviews he credits family, faith and friends for the neighborhood's stability and names the people and places that shaped him.
hilleast.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

hilleast.title: Gina Arlotto
hilleast.summary: Arlotto's family has lived on Kentucky Avenue since the 1990s. Drawing on her work in pedestrian planning, preservation and DC schools, she talks about recent changes on the Hill and how the neighborhood lived through the September 11 attacks and the January 6 riot.
hilleast.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

hilleast.title: Alvin Harris interview, 2020
hilleast.summary: Harris's family came from North Carolina in 1966, when he was eight, and settled in Hill East. He attended Bryan Elementary and Eliot Junior High, finished Eastern High in 1977, and talks about carpentry, federal work and the city under Marion Barry.

kingmanpark.title: Joseph M. Benson, Sr. interview, 2022
kingmanpark.summary: Benson moved from South Carolina in 1952. He talks about attending Spingarn High School, finding work, buying a home and raising a family, studying horticulture, his neighborhood in Kingman Park, and advances for the Black community in D.C. since the 1960s.

kingmanpark.title: Mariana and Elias Souri
kingmanpark.summary: Brother and sister who grew up on Lincoln Park with their parents and grandparents, in the house where they still lived in 2002. Their memories center on a close-knit Arabic family and the neighborhood changes that came with school integration at Hine Junior High.
kingmanpark.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

kingmanpark.title: Minnie Lee White
kingmanpark.summary: A two-page summary, not a recording. Hazel Kreinheder wrote up her 1974 talk with White, who had lived since 1932 on Massachusetts Avenue SE near Lincoln Park. It includes a story about the Capitol Hill resident who sculpted a statue of suffragists for the Capitol.
kingmanpark.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

kingmanpark.title: Lloyd Thompson
kingmanpark.summary: Thompson grew up on the 1300 block of East Capitol Street after what he calls urban removal pushed his family out of Southwest in the mid-1950s. He names families on the block, businesses, churches, theaters, old streetcar lines and buses, and later work as a cowboy out West.
kingmanpark.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

kingmanpark.title: Herbert P. Ramsey, M.D.
kingmanpark.summary: Ramsey, Eastern High School class of 1912, kept a large file on early alumni for the school's reunions. Most of this interview with Hazel Kreinheder is his memory of those students, where they lived and who their families were. He also describes his medical career.
kingmanpark.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

kingmanpark.title: Sah Brown
kingmanpark.summary: Brown was principal of Eastern High School for six years from 2016. He talks about his route into education after college basketball and the NBA minor leagues, and about Eastern's history and supportive community.
kingmanpark.archive: Ruth Ann Overbeck Capitol Hill History Project

mountpleasant.title: Mount Pleasant Riot Oral History Project
mountpleasant.summary: Ten audio interviews, with transcripts, recorded by Pat Scallen with people who were part of the community during the 1991 riot, set off by a police shooting of a Salvadoran man. They cover the riot, policing, neighborhood history, gentrification and what changed afterward.
mountpleasant.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative)

mountpleasant.title: Robert Fleming interview, 2017
mountpleasant.summary: Fleming moved to Mount Pleasant in 1975, served three terms as an ANC commissioner in the 1980s and co-founded Neighbors Consejo. He discusses the riot, gentrification, public intoxication, improvements in community policing afterward, and relations among the neighborhood's communities.
mountpleasant.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative: Mount Pleasant Riot Oral History Project)

mountpleasant.title: Pedro Avilés interview, 2017
topics: DC Latino Civil Rights Task Force
mountpleasant.summary: A Salvadoran American and longtime resident, Avilés describes arriving in Adams Morgan in 1974, the Sacred Heart Church theatre group, tensions between teachers and non-English-speaking students, the riot, and his later role as founding member and director of the DC Latino Civil Rights Task Force.
mountpleasant.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative: Mount Pleasant Riot Oral History Project)

mountpleasant.title: Arturo Griffiths interview, 2018
mountpleasant.summary: Griffiths, a longtime resident and activist born in Panama, co-founded the Latin American Youth Center. He talks about learning English, Howard University, Mayor Barry and the Latino community, how the riot affected Latinos in Mount Pleasant, and gentrification.
mountpleasant.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative: Mount Pleasant Riot Oral History Project)

mountpleasant.title: Charlene Howard interview, 2017
mountpleasant.summary: A longtime resident from one of the neighborhood's few remaining multigenerational African American families, Howard talks about growing up there, residents' political activism in the 1970s, police-community language barriers, the riot and gentrification.
mountpleasant.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative: Mount Pleasant Riot Oral History Project)

mountpleasant.title: Elinor Hart interview, 2017
mountpleasant.summary: Hart bought a home in Mount Pleasant in 1974 and has worked with the Main Street Association and Historic Mt. Pleasant. She covers changing demographics, the controversy over historic district designation, the riot, police-community relations and gentrification.
mountpleasant.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative: Mount Pleasant Riot Oral History Project)

mountpleasant.title: Alice Kelly interview, 2018
mountpleasant.summary: Kelly has lived in Mount Pleasant since 1983 and has been active in the local ANC. She describes her first impressions of the neighborhood, improvements at the elementary school, community work on the main street, and the riot.
mountpleasant.archive: Dig DC, DC Public Library (DC Oral History Collaborative: Mount Pleasant Riot Oral History Project)

mountpleasant.title: Viterbo Martinez interview, 1982
mountpleasant.summary: A barbershop owner who came to Washington from New York talks about his shop in Mount Pleasant, his immigration to the United States, the D.C. Hispanic community and groups such as Ayuda and the Catholic Hispanic Center, and education here and at home.

mountpleasant.title: Silvester Arturo interview, 1982
mountpleasant.summary: A Latino police officer in the Mt. Pleasant area describes his duties as a bilingual officer, relations between police and the community, disillusionment among Hispanic officers, and the problems and agencies of the Latino community. A two-part interview.

mountpleasant.title: Patrice Cleary interview, 2019
